title: Making robot-control models robust to real-world noise
one_liner: Train robot-control models to ignore action noise and sensory disturbances by adversarially teaching them what-breaks-them-most, in order of harm.
lead: Robot-control models (called VLAs) take images and text instructions and output arm commands. In the real world, cameras get smudged, arms get bumped, and instructions get garbled. This paper measures how badly 17 different types of real noise break today's robot models, then builds a training method that teaches a model to stay strong against whichever noise hurts it worst.

problem.h2: Robot models break when the world is messy
paras: A robot-control model (a VLA, which stands for Vision-Language-Action) takes three inputs: what the camera sees (an image), what a human says to do (a text instruction), and what the arm just did (the previous action). It outputs what the arm should do next. In clean lab conditions this works fine. But in real factories and homes, cameras fog up, arms get jostled by obstacles, microphones garble speech, and power fluctuates. Today's robot models break easily: existing defenses address only camera blur but ignore arm noise or instruction errors.

A beginner tries to just add filtered random noise during training (a standard trick). This does not work, because the 17 different types of real noise do not look like uniform randomness. Bumping an arm creates a specific kind of wrong action. A foggy camera creates a specific kind of blurred image. The model learns to ignore random noise but still fails on real noise.

callout.html: Train the model by feeding it the specific real-world noise that hurts it most (found automatically), and teach it to output the same correct action anyway.

steps.text: Test model on 17 real-world noise types (arm bumps, camera fog, etc.). Measure which noise hurts it most.
Use an exploration algorithm (UCB) to automatically pick which noise to train against next, focusing on the ones that break the model most.
For the selected noise type, create action noise that maximizes mismatch in the model's internal action-predicting function (flow matching loss).

steps.b: Train on both clean and adversarial
steps.text: Train the model's action head to output the right arm command whether inputs are clean or hit by the worst-case noise.
After learning to handle that noise, go back to step 1 and identify the next most harmful noise type.

paras: The paper modifies the action head (the neural network part that outputs arm commands) by retraining it on two objectives at once: the original clean actions and worst-case adversarial actions. The model learns weights that keep the arm command correct even when inputs are corrupted.

hidden.h2: Flow matching loss: the hidden quantity
hidden.name: Flow matching loss mismatch
paras: The hidden quantity the paper measures is flow matching loss mismatch: the gap between the error the model makes on a clean (undistorted) input and the error it makes on the same input after applying adversarial noise. A high mismatch means the noise is severely breaking the model's ability to predict the right arm action. A low mismatch means the model is ignoring that noise.

The paper estimates this mismatch by running the model on the same input pair (robot state, instruction) twice: once clean and once with perturbation applied. The difference in loss scores tells you how badly that perturbation hurts. The UCB algorithm then uses these mismatch scores to prioritize which perturbation to train against next—always picking the noise type that causes the highest mismatch.

heat.caption: Darker means higher mismatch (worse for model). True means marked as high priority for training.

reads.html: The mismatch tells you whether the model cares about a noise type. A big mismatch means this noise breaks the model badly and should be trained against immediately.

Mathematically, mismatch is computed as the L2 loss under the adversarial perturbation minus the clean loss, both evaluated on the flow matching objective. The UCB algorithm treats each perturbation type as an arm in a bandit problem, where the reward is the measured mismatch.

paras: The core idea is simple: teach the model to survive real-world noise by training it on the noise that breaks it worst first. Here is why this works.

Standard noise-augmentation training adds random noise uniformly (equal amounts of all 17 noise types). The model then learns a weak resistance to everything. But real-world noise is not uniform: an arm bump breaks the model worse than a tiny camera flicker. If you train only on arm bumps first, you teach the model the hardest lesson early. Then when you add the weaker noise types, the model already has strong foundations. Adversarial training (finding the worst-case noise for a given action) sharpens this further: instead of random noise, you feed the model the specific perturbation that maximizes its error. The model must learn weights that keep the action correct even when that worst case hits. The UCB algorithm solves the cold-start problem: it automatically tests each noise type a few times to measure harm, then doubles down on the ones that matter most.
Combining this with flow matching (a modern diffusion-based method for generating actions) ensures the resistance applies to the full action-generation process, not just a classification layer.

stages.s: UCB: test each of 17 noise types, compute mismatch
Generate worst-case action noise for top offender
Train on clean actions and adversarial actions together
Action that stays correct despite trained noise types

math.h2: The training objective with adversarial noise
math.words: Train against a combination of clean action loss and noisy action loss. The noisy action is the adversarial perturbation that maximizes the mismatch. Balance both with a weighting parameter.
math.equation: Loss_robust = L(model, clean_action) + lambda * L(model, adversarial_action) where adversarial_action = argmax_delta L(model, action + delta)
symbols: the flow matching loss: how badly the model predicts this action
the true action from the demonstration
the action plus noise that maximizes the model's error
the weight balancing clean vs adversarial robustness, set to trade off accuracy for robustness

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose true action is move-arm-to (0.5, 0.3). Clean loss is 0.2.
Adversarial bump noise creates perturbed action (0.7, 0.5). Model's loss on that is 1.8 (big error).
Adversarial loss is 1.8, clean loss is 0.2.
Training adjusts weights to shrink this 2.0 loss. Model learns to predict (0.5, 0.3) even when the input bump noise is present.
With trained weights, adversarial loss drops to 0.4 (model now resistant to that bump), while clean loss stays 0.2.

math.note: The perturbation delta is found by gradient-based search (PGD), not random guessing, so it reliably targets the worst case.

bars.h2: Success rate gains across multiple noise types

charts.title: Naive training (all noise types equally weighted)
charts.note: Model trained on random uniform noise fails badly when real noise hits. No noise type gets strong protection.

charts.title: RobustVLA (UCB-prioritized adversarial training)
charts.note: Model trained on worst-first adversarial noise stays strong across all three noise types. Clean accuracy only drops slightly (94 to 92), a good tradeoff.

items.html: If you train only on the 17 noise types seen during development, the model might memorize those specific noises. Real-world perturbations are infinite. The paper does test generalization to unseen noise types (like external forces), and shows the model's resistance carries over, but there are limits.

The UCB algorithm picks the worst noise first. But if the worst noise is extreme (e.g., motor failure), the model might overfit to handling that one case and neglect moderate noise types. Tuning UCB parameters (exploration coefficient, window size) is needed.

Finding worst-case noise via PGD (gradient-based search) requires many loss evaluations. The paper uses PGD with multiple steps, which adds training time. On large-scale robots this could be prohibitive.
When UCB parameters are tuned and the perturbation budget is realistic, the model learns to survive noise types it has never seen before and works on real robots, as the paper demonstrates.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A demo should train a small robot-control model on a simple task (e.g., moving an arm to a target) with two variants: (1) baseline trained on random noise only, (2) this paper's method with UCB-guided adversarial training. Then, introduce new noise types at test time (e.g., a force bump while the model is running, or a corrupted image) and measure success rate. The trained model should keep working; the baseline should fail.
demo.metric_eq: success_rate = (number of correct final arm positions) / (total test trials)
demo.closing: The demo should show that UCB-guided worst-case training beats uniform noise training on both seen and unseen perturbations, and that the trained model stays accurate on clean inputs while the baseline does not.
